title: How cooperative relationships form, persist, and fall apart.
text:
Research


How cooperative relationships form, persist, and fall apart.


Broadly I am interested in the evolution of cooperative social behaviors. Below is a list of some of my current projects, but my work extends beyond these as well! I am always thinking about how I can apply my experience with these projects to other research questions and systems, if you have ideas let me know!










Ongoing projects





01



Colony level social relations models


Fitting a STRAND social-relations model across all of our long-term data, separating reciprocity, kinship, and individual generosity in grooming and food sharing, and watching how bonds change over time.


STRANDBayesian networksReciprocityR / Stan



                                                                                        


A colony as a directed network — who gives to whom, and how much. Modelled with STRAND (Ross, McElreath & Redhead 2024).




OngoingAnalysis




02



Automatic bat ID with machine learning


Building a computer-vision pipeline to re-identify individual bats from video, testing whether 21 individuals are visually separable on held-out days, so we can study behavior without hand labelling days of footage.


Computer visionRe-identificationPythonAutomation







OngoingMethod dev




03



Defection & partner choice


Experimentally manipulating whether a new bat in the colony is helpful or defective, then measuring how bats differentially invest in them: a direct causal test of reciprocity and partner-choice.


Captive experimentPartner choiceFasting trials



Grooming Food shared Bond strength






Two strangers join the colony





Ongoing




04



Defection & interdependence


How does response to defection change when bats are also siblings? Or what if they have been long term friends? Or what if the defective bat is their only option? These are all examples of what we might label as “interdependence”, and we want to understand how bats respond to defection differently in these scenarios. The prediction, animated below: after the same defection, an unrelated bat withdraws its investment, while between kin interdependence buffers the response and the focal bat keeps giving.


KinshipInterdependenceCaptive experiment



Food shared Defection Bond strength





Unrelated pair





Reciprocal food sharing






Kin pair · siblings





Reciprocal food sharing







Ongoing

















From the field to the lab


The bats I study are wild-caught or donated from zoos. The science happens in the lab.


I work with captive colonies of vampire bats: running fasting trials, tracking who shares food with whom, and testing what makes a cooperative bond form and hold. Once the animals are with us, the lab is where they stay. We make sure they are happy and engaged in their new home though! They are well cared for, and often are in better condition than those in the field.


We don’t release vampire bats back to the wild, so the colony has to be a place where bats can live, roost, and socialize naturally enough that the cooperation I measure is the real thing. Good husbandry isn’t a side task: it’s the foundation the entire research program stands on.











Context




Study system


Common vampire bats (Desmodus rotundus), studied in captive colonies (animals that are wild-caught or donated from zoos).




Methods


Bayesian social-relations models (STRAND / Stan), longitudinal network analysis in R, RFID tracking, machine-learning re-ID, and manipulative fasting-trial experiments.




People & support


Advised by Dr. Gerry Carter (Carter Lab), studying cooperation in captive colonies of vampire bats. Earlier training with the Pfennig Lab (UNC) and Sheehan Lab (Cornell).










Five quick answers


The questions I actually get asked



Do vampire bats really share blood?


Yes. A bat that fed regurgitates part of its meal to a roost-mate that didn’t, and it’s often not a relative. It’s one of the clearest cases of reciprocal cooperation in any animal: bats keep track of who has helped them and preferentially help those partners back (Wilkinson 1984, Carter & Wilkinson 2013). That bookkeeping is what my research is about.




Will a vampire bat attack me?


No. Common vampire bats mostly feed on sleeping livestock, take about a tablespoon of blood, and the animal usually never notices. They’re shy, only weigh ~40 g, and far more interested in cow blood than mine!




How do you tell individual bats apart in the dark?


Three ways: tiny RFID tags logged at feeders, forearm bands readable on infrared video, and (the part I’m actively building) computer-vision models that learn to re-identify individuals and score their interactions automatically.




Are the odds in the game real?


Every probability is taken from published field and lab studies: Wilkinson’s classic starvation and food-sharing data and the reciprocity experiments from the Carter Lab. Sources and simplifications are listed under “How the odds work” on the Play page and on the vampire bat science page.




Can you give a talk, or can I collaborate?


Probably, I love outreach! If you or anyone you know is interested in hearing about vampire bat friendships I’m happy to talk all day about it. Email me, I will reply within two days.



PublicationsFeel the dilemma, play the game

title: You are a vampire bat.
text:
A survival game · the odds come from real vampire bat studies
You are a vampire bat.
You are a young vampire bat. Each night, bite a sleeping cow or go hungry.
Two empty nights in a row and you have no blood left, so you have to beg or starve,
and only the friends you groomed and fed will feed you. Choose where you sleep, who you groom, and who
you save. Survive ten nights.

🦇 Begin the first night
Learn the real science →

Every run is recorded anonymously: your choices, never your name. The logs describe how people play and will one day let the other bats hunt with real players' strategies.



















Post to leaderboard
Play again






Top seasons
Show 
Current game
Before the relaunch (up to 3 Sept 2026)





#
Player
Species
Score
Survived
When




Loading scores…







Achievements 

Earned once per browser, kept between seasons. Three are secret.





How the odds work

Where the numbers come from. Every number in this game is read from one data
file, bat-data.js, and every entry there carries either a citation or a
model flag with its design reasoning written beside it. Where a
field study gives a number, the game uses it. Where no field analog exists, the constant is
flagged and its reasoning is stated; no constant ships with neither. That is a deliberate policy
choice, and it is disclosed here rather than hidden. These notes read the same file, so what you
read here cannot drift from what you play against. Full references are on the
Learn more page.

Sourced numbers. Adult bats fail to feed on about
7% of nights; bats under two years
old fail on roughly a third (Wilkinson 1984). You start young: your hidden hunting skill is drawn
around a 28% fail rate and improves
by ×0.93 with every fed night, down to a
floor of 8%, the direction real
juveniles learn in. Roughly 60 fasting hours is fatal (Wilkinson 1984; McNab 1973), so you begin
with two nights of fuel, and any
unfed night costs one, or
1.5 in rain, in the storms, or
after a flight to the far valley, whether or not a bite was ever rolled. When your reserve hits
zero, each roost-mate who fed that night rescues you with
P = 0.02 + 0.60 × bond,
capped at 0.9: real donations track
prior grooming and sharing, not kinship alone (Wilkinson 1984; Carter & Wilkinson 2013).
You do not have to hit zero to be fed: on any unfed night, a present partner who ate and trusts you
at least 0.70 brings up part of
her meal with P 0.35
(0.5 blood,
10 points), which is what a
couple of close friends are for; the values are model. Donations are
graded, a sip to a full crop, and build bonds in proportion; grooming escalates into sharing (Carter
et al. 2020). Regurgitation is one bout of one meal, so you can bring up
one donation a dawn, a second only
while your crop is still nearly full, and blood is never free to give: whatever is left in your crop
at the season's end scores 45
points per unit, and flying out with 1
or less adds 12 points to your fail
chance (a bat on empty hunts worse; model). Grooming runs well beyond hygienic need and tracks partnerships
(Wilkinson 1986; Carter & Leffer 2015), and it keeps the mites off: below
0.5 fur they move in and drain
0.5 blood a night (Lewis 1995).
Bright moonlight suppresses vampire bat foraging (Crespo, Burns, Mitchell & Linhart 1972,
J Mammal 53:366-368; Saldaña-Vázquez & Munguía-Rosas 2013): a bright night adds
10 points to every bat's fail chance
and a dim one 5; the magnitudes are
model. Bonded bats forage together and find each other by
individually distinctive contact calls (Ripperger & Carter 2021; Carter et al. 2012; Carter
& Wilkinson 2016), which is why the bat already at a wound is one of your roost-mates
50% of the time.

The pasture. Each night the paddock deals
one to
five animals (most often three; how many
of a herd sleep within reach is never the same twice) from three tiers, and size is the legend:

Calf: meal 0.75,
thin skin (bite −4%), occupied
10% of the time. Real vampires
hit calves and the most accessible animals first (Turner 1975); the values are
model.
Steer: meal 1.0,
the standard dinner, occupied 25%
of the time.
Prime cow: meal 1.5,
and someone usually got there first: occupied
55% of the time on night
one, rising 3 points a
night to 75%, because
favored hosts are re-attacked night after night and old wounds reopened (Greenhall 1972; Turner
1975); the occupancy curve is model.

A full meal is 40 to 60% of a bat's body mass, 15 to 25 mL (Greenhall 1972; McFarland &
Wimsatt 1969); the in-game scale is relative, model. Reopening a
wound another bat opened is near-instant (Greenhall 1972), so any bite at a contested or waited
wound is 5 points easier.
Wilkinson's failure rates are measured per night and a disturbed herd is abandoned (Greenhall,
Schmidt & Lopez-Forment 1971), so you get exactly
one bite roll a night: a miss wakes
the herd and the hunt is over. The far valley, open on nights
3 to
8, is the gamble: it deals its own
one to
five animals with prime cows weighted
×2, cattle nobody bleeds are
fatter (meals ×1.3), few bats
fly that far (occupancy ×0.5),
and a meal taken there pays 12 extra
points. Against that, your bite is +10%
more likely to fail and a hungry night costs the
1.5 blood flight. In the sim the
far valley leaves the expected score unchanged but raises the ceiling and the death rate:
several-kilometer excursions are routine (Wilkinson 1985a); every value is
model. Sleeping at the valley outpost scouts the far herd (bite
−3% there).

Dark hours. Each night gives you
three dark hours,
two in the storms: a
model framing of usable darkness, since feeding bouts run 9 to 40
minutes and several bouts a night are observed (Greenhall 1972; Wilkinson 1985a). Approaching an
animal costs one hour, each wait costs one, and at zero you fly home unfed. Squalls
(7% of nights
3 to
8, bite
+18%) and the storm finale (bite
+15%) are
model, with the energetic direction from McNab 1973. A rich night
(8% of dark, calm nights) is bite
−5% and meal
+0.25, also
model. The status bar's Skill stat is your chance of landing a
bite tonight with every term folded in (your skill, the moon, the weather, the far valley, an open
wound, fever, hunger, the luck damper); hover or tap it for the itemized list. Dark hours themselves
are not shown as a bar: the pasture line tells you how many are left.

The encounter. If another bat is at the wound you have four verbs.
Join is tolerated with
P = 0.05 + 0.50 × bond;
a stranger gets the base 5%.
Simultaneous feeding is rare in the field, 5 cases in 36.6 hours across 65 bats, mostly mother and
young (Wilkinson 1985a), and bond predicts who forages together (Ripperger & Carter 2021);
the slope is model. A refusal is a feeding-place confrontation
call, no injury, and that animal is done with you tonight (Sailler & Schmidt 1978, a captive
study, cited as such). Tolerated, you co-feed and the bond warms
+0.05 on both sides (Ripperger
& Carter 2021; Carter et al. 2020). Displace wins
50% of the time against a
young stranger, 30% against
an adult and 15% against
a dominant one; a roost-mate rolls as an adult
(30%), the attempt costs
−0.10 bond win or lose, and
she remembers. Larger bats displace smaller ones at a wound, an adult male over a yearling
(Wilkinson 1985a); nobody is ever hurt, the loser lifts away; the odds are
model. A stranger's rank stays hidden until you have joined or
pushed her, then it sits on a chip: that is how displacements at a feeder reveal a hierarchy, and
since no female roost rank exists (Crisp, Brent & Carter 2021), rank here is feeder-scoped
only. Wait: bouts end, so she leaves with P
0.5 each dark hour, and the drained
wound then yields 0.5 less (never
below 0.5); sequential feeding at one
wound is observed (Wilkinson 1985a), the drain is model.
Leave costs nothing beyond the hour already spent.

The roosts. Vampire bats use several roost trees and move between them
(Wilkinson 1985a). Each game draws 3 or
4 roosts, the hollow you were born in and
the rest, and every one is an independent bundle: 4
to 16 residents (around
8), a hidden generosity, a hidden
disease risk and a hidden aggression risk, all model. No roost is the
good one by design; you learn a roost by sleeping in it, and after one dawn its card shows who lives
there and what you saw. From night 2 you choose where to sleep on the flight home, after the hunt,
so the bats who can feed you if you came home empty are the ones at the roost you pick; night 1 and
the storm nights lock you to the hollow. Every night every bat sleeps at home unless the season's
switching roll (drawn between 2%
and 12% a night, far-rangers
×3) sends her to another
roost, so a friend is sometimes not where you expect her and a stranger sometimes is; in the storms
nobody switches. Your first dawn somewhere new, the residents groom you back at half rate and no one
shares with a beggar they trust below 0.30;
anywhere, only bats who trust you at least
0.10 will feed you when
you beg, because sharing happens among familiar associates (Wilkinson 1984). At dawn you may fall
sick, P = 0.02 + 0.05 × crowding + 0.08 × the
roost's disease score, ×1.5 on a
first visit and ×0.5 at home:
two dawns of one less action
and half the groom-backs. Sick bats groom less and are groomed less (Stockmaier, Bolnick, Page
& Carter 2018; Ripperger, Stockmaier & Carter 2020); the rates are
model. Or a resident may bite you,
P = 0.01 + 0.10 × the
aggression score, ×2 while you
are the stranger and 0 when a bat you trust at least
0.50 hangs beside you:
0.5 blood at once and
two dawns of a stiff wing
(residents guard a roost against strangers, Wilkinson 1985b; rates model).
Mites are a separate roll with a separate cure. The valley outpost overlooks the far valley and
scouts it: bite −3% there.

The year. Two things have already happened to the colony when a season opens,
and they hold all ten nights: one that
favours a couple of close friends (a rough year of scarred males, a stingy year where only close
friends feed a beggar, a sickly year, a quiet year of half-empty roosts) and one that favours a wide
circle (a generous year, a restless year of roost-hopping, a crowded year, a lean year of thin
herds). You read them once, in the first dusk's briefing, and their icons stay in the status bar.
Each is a trade: the sim holds every year's median score within 5% of the others, so there is no
good year to refresh for, only a different one. Two more surprises land on random nights
between 4 and
8, drawn from a deck of twelve
(hunters, a big storm, cattle disease, plague, dominant bats, injured ears, a cattle drive, drought,
newcomers, a mite bloom, bright nights, a cold snap); each pops up with its own sound the night it
lands and sits in the status bar while it runs. The culls, storms and roost invasions have field
analogs (Wilkinson 1985a, 1985b); the amounts are model.

The season. No two seasons pay off the same way, so a single habit cannot win
every game. Four more things are drawn once per season and deliberately not shown: you
read them from what happens. Contagion:
every bat you groom or share with is a contact, with
46% per contact at full
contagion and ×5 if she is
coughing; coughing bats are marked on the network, groom back at half rate, and appear more often
in roosts with a high disease score. Sick bats groom less and are groomed less (Stockmaier, Bolnick,
Page & Carter 2018; Ripperger, Stockmaier & Carter 2020); the rates are
model. The rescue curve: the chance a fed bat feeds you when
you beg is P = 0.02 + 0.60 × bondk,
with k drawn between 0.6 and
2: a tight season (k high)
rewards a couple of very close partners, an open season (k low) rewards a wide circle. The partner
panel shows each bat's chance under this season's curve, so the shape is there to be read. Donation
tracks relationship strength (Carter & Wilkinson 2013); the exponent is
model. Attention: you can keep
3 to
7 real bonds warm; beyond
that every bond fades an extra
0.015 a night per extra
bond, and the dawn panel says so. Grooming budgets are finite (Wilkinson 1986); the numbers are
model. Switching: the colony's nightly roost-switching rate
is drawn between 2% and
12%, so in some seasons a wide
circle hedges your friends' absences and in others it is wasted. A meal for a hungry (not starving)
bat pays 11 points and builds bond
with diminishing returns, while a save pays in full; with one donation a dawn, each has to be worth
making.

The luck damper, and desperate hours. One constant is pure engineering, and it
is labeled that way here. After two
straight unfed nights your next bite is
10 points easier, and the night
says so: you fly careful tonight. It has no field analog and the game does not pretend it
has one. Its reason is variance capping: in a
ten-night run, two bad rolls must not
become a death spiral you never chose. Separately, when your reserve is at
1 or below, the high-variance
options (an occupied prime cow, the far valley) turn amber and read desperate hours, the
energy-budget rule, risk-prone under deficit (Stephens 1981). Since the 2026-09-04 relaunch this is
no longer framing only: flying out that hungry adds the
12-point hungry term to your
bite, itemized in the Skill stat.

Plausible, for play (invented for the game, flagged so you know): the learning
rate, bond decay (0.02 a night), your two
old friends starting at a bond of 0.55
or more and the rest of the hollow lower, every roost's hidden bundle, roost-mates' hidden
personalities (big-hearted, tight-furred, far-ranger, thin), close friends bringing you part of a
meal on a hungry night, and roost-mates rescuing each other through their own friendships. Roost-mates can genuinely starve: a begging bat
that no one feeds, including you, dies, and its friendships die with it.

Score and balance. Score is a fitness ledger: nights survived, feeds (a prime
cow fed alone and a far-valley meal pay extra), co-feeds, displacements, donations scaled by size
and need, lives saved, and at the season's end a survival bonus, your bonds valued the way the
season values them (bondk, summed), your single deepest bond
(×45), every partner who ever fed
you (12 each), the blood left in
your crop (×45), and a full-roost
bonus if nobody in the hollow died. Death keeps the ledger you earned. The 2026-09-04 relaunch
rebuilt this economy because players had found that handing blood to every bat every night was
always best: the leaderboard restarted that day, and the earlier board is kept under
Before the relaunch. sim/batsim4.py Monte-Carlos 20,000 seasons per policy
from the same data file. Medians for a bat who never leaves the hollow: sharing widely 716 in an open
season and 557 in a tight one; keeping two close friends 694 and 645; never giving blood 670 and 614.
So a wide circle wins open and low-contagion seasons, a couple of close friends wins tight and
high-contagion ones, and the years swing that gap by up to 80 points either way. Every year's median
sits within 5% of the others; survival runs 63 to 68% for the sensible styles; a roost wound decides
under 3% of deaths. The far valley, always taken, scores the same median as never going (639 against
646) with a higher ceiling and a survival rate of 57% against 64%: a real gamble, not a trap. Only
flagged constants were tuned to get there; no cited number moved.

What gets recorded. Every run writes an anonymous log: each choice you make, the state of your bat when you made it, and how the night turned out. It carries a random id for this browser so your separate runs can be told apart from other people's, and nothing else: no name, no exact time, no device details. The leaderboard name you type is never joined to it. The logs are used in aggregate to describe how people play this game and which strategies do well, and later to let the other bats hunt with strategies drawn from real players. Only summaries will ever be published.

title: A service economy on a coral reef.
text:
← Play the vampire bat game
The real science · cleaner wrasse
A service economy on a coral reef.
The cleaner-wrasse mutualism is one of the best-studied cooperation systems
in nature: a marketplace with clients, cheating, punishment, and reputation.
Here's the science behind each mechanic.







Two thousand clients a day
The bluestreak cleaner wrasse (Labroides dimidiatus) holds a small territory, a
"cleaning station," where other fish come to have their ectoparasites picked off. A single
cleaner inspects on the order of 2,300 clients per day and eats over a
thousand parasites doing it1. Clients queue, pose with fins
spread, and hold still for a stranger's mouth. Both sides profit, as long as both sides
behave.

The temptation
Here's the catch that makes it a cooperation problem: given the choice, cleaners
prefer client mucus over parasites2. Every
honest inspection is a small act of self-restraint. Cheating (biting mucus) makes the client
visibly jolt, which is what makes the system measurable in the field.

Partner control
What keeps cleaners honest is that clients have options. Resident clients
with small home ranges are stuck with their local cleaner, and they respond to cheats by
punishing (chasing the cleaner around the coral, which costs it foraging time).
Visitors with large ranges simply leave and take their custom to a rival
station3. Cleaners essentially never cheat
predatory clients, where the "punishment" would be getting eaten.

Reputation
Bystander clients observe ongoing interactions and use what they see. In experiments,
clients preferentially approached cleaners they had watched cooperating and avoided ones they
had seen cheat4. A cleaner's honesty toward the client in
front of it is simultaneously an advertisement to everyone in line, which is why, in the game,
cheating with a bystander present costs future customers.

The massage
A cleaner can also hover above a client and drum its pelvic fins along the client's back, a
"massage" that provides no food. Experiments show cleaners use it strategically to entice new
partners, calm predators, and reconcile with clients they've just cheated
5. The touch itself is a genuine service because it measurably
lowers client stress hormones6.

← Play the game


References

Grutter, A.S. (1996). Parasite removal rates by the cleaner wrasse Labroides dimidiatus. Marine Ecology Progress Series 130, 61–70. doi:10.3354/meps130061
Grutter, A.S. & Bshary, R. (2003). Cleaner wrasse prefer client mucus: support for partner control mechanisms in cleaning interactions. Proceedings of the Royal Society B 270 (Suppl.), S242–S244. doi:10.1098/rsbl.2003.0077
Bshary, R. & Grutter, A.S. (2002). Asymmetric cheating opportunities and partner control in a cleaner fish mutualism. Animal Behaviour 63, 547–555. doi:10.1006/anbe.2001.1937
Bshary, R. & Grutter, A.S. (2006). Image scoring and cooperation in a cleaner fish mutualism. Nature 441, 975–978. doi:10.1038/nature04755
Bshary, R. & Würth, M. (2001). Cleaner fish Labroides dimidiatus manipulate client reef fish by providing tactile stimulation. Proceedings of the Royal Society B 268, 1495–1501. doi:10.1098/rspb.2001.1495

title: Blood, friendship, and bookkeeping.
text:
← Back to the game
The real science · vampire bat
Blood, friendship, and bookkeeping.
Everything in the game comes from real studies of real bats. Here's the
natural history behind each mechanic, and where the science is still open.







The diet
The common vampire bat (Desmodus rotundus) feeds only on blood, mostly from
sleeping livestock, taking a few teaspoons in a 20-minute meal. The part that makes it really
tough on the bats? Blood is nearly all water and protein, so bats can't store much energy.
Gerald Wilkinson's foundational field study in Costa Rica found that adult bats come home
hungry on about 7% of nights (young bats fail far more, on up to a third of
nights), and a bat that goes roughly 3 nights without a meal starves to
death1. Every bat in a colony lives two bad nights
away from risking death.

The bonds
Wilkinson's 1984 Nature paper reported something remarkable: bats that fed
regurgitate part of their blood meal to roost-mates that didn't. The donation costs the donor
but can buy the recipient about another 12 hours of life1.
Crucially, sharing wasn't limited to mothers and pups or close kin. Unrelated adults shared
too, and they shared preferentially with the individuals who had shared with them before. It
became one of the textbook cases of reciprocity in animals.

The ones who invested are the ones who get rescued
Thirty years later, Gerry Carter and Wilkinson tested the reciprocity claim with controlled
fasting experiments in a captive colony. They withheld food from one bat at a time and watched
who fed it. The best predictor of receiving food was not relatedness, but the amount of food
and grooming that bat had previously given to its potential donors
2. In the game, your rescue probability is built from your
bonds (P = 0.02 + 0.60 × bond, counted over each roost-mate that fed that night). Help comes
back from the relationships you've built, and only a bat with blood can give any away.

Grooming
Vampire bats groom each other far more than the hygienic baseline other species
show4. Grooming removes ectoparasites like bat flies and
mites5 (the game's mite mechanic), but it's also a social cue.
When Carter introduced strangers to each other in captivity, new relationships developed by
escalation. Bats began with low-cost grooming, "testing the water," and only
later graduated to food sharing if that bat groomed them
back3. That's what the game rewards when grooming builds the
bond that later makes sharing (and rescue) likely.

Nights with a bright moon
Vampire bats are creatures of the dark in a strict sense. Field observations in México
found that Desmodus forages far less on bright moonlit nights, concentrating activity
into the darkest hours6. This is a pattern called lunar
phobia, seen across many Neotropical bats, most plausibly as predator avoidance. The game's
moon cycle comes from that finding. The direction of the effect is sourced; the size
of the penalty on a bright night is the game's own tuning, and the storm nights that close
each season are dramatized. In reality, there is no "end" for feeding at the end of the
season, these parts just make the game more fun from a user perspective.

How much to give?
Donations aren't all-or-nothing. Donors regurgitate for varying durations, and the amount
transferred varies with the relationship and the donor's own condition
1,2. The sip / meal / full-crop choice in
the game reflects the bat's choice in generosity. Bigger gifts build bonds faster but cost
more of your own safety margin, so are more of a gamble!

What we still don't know
The open questions are the fun ones. Should a bat concentrate on a few strong bonds or
spread across many weak ones? How do reciprocity and fitness interdependence (having
a genuine stake in a partner's survival) interact? What happens to a relationship after a
partner defects? These are live research questions, and they're the ones
my own work tackles with long-term colony data, social-network
models, and manipulative experiments. The game's dilemmas are the real dilemmas. The optimal
strategy is genuinely unsolved.

← Play the game


References

Wilkinson, G.S. (1984). Reciprocal food sharing in the vampire bat. Nature 308, 181–184. doi:10.1038/308181a0
Carter, G.G. & Wilkinson, G.S. (2013). Food sharing in vampire bats: reciprocal help predicts donations more than relatedness or harassment. Proceedings of the Royal Society B 280, 20122573. doi:10.1098/rspb.2012.2573
Carter, G.G., Farine, D.R., Crisp, R.J., Vrtilek, J.K., Ripperger, S.P. & Page, R.A. (2020). Development of new food-sharing relationships in vampire bats. Current Biology 30, 1275–1279. doi:10.1016/j.cub.2020.01.055
Carter, G.G. & Leffer, L. (2015). Social grooming in bats: are vampire bats exceptional? PLoS ONE 10, e0138430. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0138430
Wilkinson, G.S. (1986). Social grooming in the common vampire bat, Desmodus rotundus. Animal Behaviour 34, 1880–1889. doi:10.1016/S0003-3472(86)80274-3
Crespo, R.F., Linhart, S.B., Burns, R.J. & Mitchell, G.C. (1972). Foraging behavior of the common vampire bat related to moonlight. Journal of Mammalogy 53, 366–368. doi:10.2307/1379175

About
I'm a second year PhD student working on vampire-bat friendship experiments in the Carter Lab at Princeton. The research page covers what I do, while this one is about how I got here. I didn't always know this is what I wanted to do! Scroll down to see my journey.

Salisbury, North Carolina · hometown
I grew up here and always loved the surrounding wildlife! Even though I wasn't exposed to much research here, I found my way in anyway.


NC School of Science & Mathematics, Durham · high school
NCSSM got me out of Salisbury, and mentorship there put me in a real research lab before I had finished high school. That first taste of science and real data was the thing that stuck.


UNC Chapel Hill · B.S. Biology, 2021–2025
Four years in Karin Pfennig's lab working on behavioral variation and hybridization in spadefoot toads. It was where I learned how to do independent research. The exploratory-behavior assays I set up are still used in the lab. I earned Highest Honors and the Robert Coker Award during my time there.


Southwestern Research Station, Arizona · undergrad field seasons
Fieldwork for the spadefoot project, comparing exploratory and hybridization behaviors across populations from Arizona to Kansas, based out of SWRS in the Chiricahua Mountains. The sky-island canyons are also where much of my photography comes from.


Cornell University · summer 2024
A summer with the Sheehan Lab studying territory and anxiety-related behavior in rewilded laboratory mice, with Dr. Matthew Zipple. This is where my passion for social behaviors developed, and also where I was involved in one of my first papers!


Gamboa, Panamá · the second colony
One of our two vampire-bat colonies lives in Gamboa. Our lab goes there to collect and study vampire bats at larger scales. The colonies here are studied simultaneously with the ones in Princeton so we can compare our findings.


Princeton University · PhD, 2025–present
Now. Ecology & Evolutionary Biology in the Carter Lab: one colony here (soon two), defection experiments, social-relations models, and a computer-vision pipeline in progress.







Salisbury, North Carolina










How I work


I split my time between three modes:


hands-on behavioral experiments with captive colonies of vampire bats
statistical modeling in R (Bayesian social-network models, mostly via STRAND)
building tools like a machine-learning pipeline to identify individual bats from video, letting us collect behavior at a scale hand-scoring can’t reach


Beyond the science


I care a lot about who gets to do science. As a first-generation bachelors and PhD student, and an openly gay researcher from a community that was underserved by science outreach, I try to build the kind of inclusive, welcoming spaces I once needed. When I’m not with the bats, I’m often behind a camera. I started doing wildlife photography while out in the field in Arizona: I figured since I was lucky enough to be surrounded by these animals I should also take pictures to showcase them to others!

title: A month to live, a colony to serve.
text:
← Play the vampire bat game
The real science · honeybee
A month to live, a colony to serve.
Honeybee workers look selfless, but the hive is policed for a reason.







A short life in stages
A summer worker honeybee lives roughly 2–5 weeks as an adult
1. She moves through jobs in a pretty reliable pattern. Young
bees nurse brood and build comb deep in the interior, middle-aged bees guard and process food,
the oldest bees forage2. The dangerous job is saved for last,
when a worker has the least life left to lose, which is exactly the trade-off the game hands
you each week.

Foraging
Foraging feeds the colony but kills the forager. Once a bee starts flying field trips she
faces predators, weather, exhaustion, and even windshields. Marked-bee studies measured the
mortality of foragers and found it strong enough that a forager's remaining life expectancy is
only a few days3. Foragers rarely die in the hive, they simply
fail to come home. In the game, every foraging trip adds 12% to your weekly death risk.

The temptation
Workers can lay unfertilized eggs that develop into males. Genetically, a
worker is more related to her own sons (r = 0.5) than to the queen's sons, her brothers
(r = 0.25), so from her genes' point of view, sneaking eggs into the comb beats raising the
queen's. So why don't all of the workers just lay their own eggs?

The police
Because the queen mates with many males, the other workers are mostly half-sisters,
and a half-sister's son (r ≈ 0.125) is worth less to them than the queen's son (r = 0.25). So
workers stop each other from reproducing4. Ratnieks
and Visscher showed that eggs laid by workers are found and eaten within a day (about
98% of them), while queen-laid eggs are left alone5.
Because of this, a laid egg is worth 0.02 × 30 = 0.6 expected points vs. 3 for honest work.

The bees take a different route to cooperation than the vampire bats' reciprocity or the
cleaner fish's reputation. Comparing them is exactly why the games exist. The question of how
cooperation is stabilized runs through my own research too.

← Play the game


References

Seeley, T.D. (1982). Adaptive significance of the age polyethism schedule in honeybee colonies. Behavioral Ecology and Sociobiology 11, 287–293. doi:10.1007/BF00299306
Visscher, P.K. & Dukas, R. (1997). Survivorship of foraging honey bees. Insectes Sociaux 44, 1–5. doi:10.1007/s000400050017
